# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Leilisk Facade Systems, Inc. / Seineix Glassworks LLC: issues review of the supply documentation

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed all six documents in the folder:

- Supply Agreement dated January 15, 2024 (the **SA**)
- October 18, 2023 Term Sheet (the **TS**)
- Quality Agreement dated January 15, 2024 (the **QA**)
- Amended and Restated Order Form No. 1 dated May 11, 2026 (the **OF**)
- Seineix press release of September 9, 2025
- Mutual NDA dated August 21, 2023

The SA is governed by New York law (SA §22.1). Its key commercial terms are:

- **Term.** The Initial Term is **60 months** from January 15, 2024, so it expires in **January 2029** (OF §2.1; SA §2.1).
- **Minimum volume.** Leilisk must buy at least **400,000 square feet of Glass Products per Contract Year** (SA §4.1).
- **Shortfall rate.** The shortfall rate is **$4.25/sq ft** (OF §5.2). A total shortfall therefore costs up to about **$1.7 million per Contract Year**.

I found five issues. Two are urgent:

- **Change of control.** The pending Ostrander acquisition is expected to close this quarter, and Seineix's consent does not appear to have been obtained (Issue 1).
- **Price objection.** Leilisk's objection to the 2026 price increase appears to have been late (Issue 2).

The other three are structural:

- The warranty is narrowed by the QA (Issue 3).
- Exclusivity is far broader than the deal agreed in the TS (Issue 4).
- There is a five-year evergreen renewal (Issue 5).

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1: Pending Ostrander acquisition triggers Seineix's change-of-control consent right (urgent)

**Where:**
- SA §16.2 (Change of Control) and §1.1 ("Change of Control", "Affiliate")
- OF §6.2 (Billing and Notices: Buyer Corporate Update)

**What the documents say:**
- **Consent required.** SA §16.2 treats a Change of Control of either party as an assignment. It therefore requires the other party's prior written consent.
- **Status of the deal.** OF §6.2 records that Leilisk signed a definitive agreement dated **April 28, 2026** under which it is to be acquired by **Ostrander Building Group, Inc.** Closing is expected in **Q4 2026**.
- **No consent on file.** Nothing in the folder shows that Seineix's consent was requested or given. Recording the deal in a billing clause is not a consent, and SA §21.4 requires any waiver to be in writing and signed.

**Why it matters:**
- **Termination right.** If closing occurs without consent, Seineix may terminate on 30 days' notice. It can do so at any time within 90 days after it learns of the Change of Control.
- **Shortfall payment.** On termination, Seineix may also demand the **Minimum Purchase Shortfall for the current Contract Year and every remaining Contract Year of the Initial Term**, calculated as if Leilisk bought nothing in those future years.
  - If closing occurs in Q4 2026, the payment covers Contract Year 3 (the shortfall actually incurred) plus Contract Years 4 and 5 (the full shortfall).
  - At $4.25/sq ft, that is roughly **$3.4 million for the two future years alone**, plus any current-year shortfall.
  - The payment is carved out of the consequential-damages exclusion (SA §13.1(c)) and survives termination (SA §17.3).
- **Supply risk.** Leilisk would also lose its contracted glass supply mid-project.
- **Ostrander group pulled in.** After closing, Ostrander will "control" Leilisk. Ostrander and its group therefore become Leilisk "Affiliates". SA §3.1 requires Leilisk to cause its Affiliates to buy **all** their Glass Products from Seineix. A consented closing could therefore still put Leilisk in breach unless this point is carved out.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Confirm with deal counsel today whether consent was sought. Check whether it is a closing condition or covenant in the April 28 acquisition agreement.
2. Before closing, obtain Seineix's signed written consent and waiver of its §16.2 rights for the Ostrander transaction.
3. In the same instrument, confirm that the §3.1 exclusivity and §4.1 minimum apply only to Leilisk's own business and not to Ostrander or its other subsidiaries.
4. If consent is refused or conditioned, the parties need to:
   - consider the price of a negotiated consent or a deferred closing; and
   - reflect the shortfall exposure in the purchase price, indemnity or escrow.

---

### Issue 2: Objection to the 2026 price adjustment was out of time

**Where:**
- SA §5.3 (Objection) and §5.2 (Price Adjustments)
- OF §3.2–3.4 (Pricing Basis)

**What the documents say:**
- **The deadline.** Leilisk may object within **30 days after receipt** of a Price Adjustment Notice. If it does not, the adjustment is **"deemed accepted"** and Leilisk loses the benchmarking process and its right to terminate the affected products.
- **The dates.**
  - OF §3.2 records that the notice was **received by Buyer on March 4, 2026**. The window therefore closed on **April 3, 2026**.
  - Leilisk's objection letter is dated **April 20, 2026** (OF §3.3). That is **17 days late**.
- **The reservations.** OF §3.3 records that Leilisk signed under reservation of rights and does not accept the Column B prices. It also records that Seineix does not waive its position.

**Why it matters:**
- **Size of the increase.** The notice raises prices on all IGUs and laminated glass by roughly 11–14%. For example, triple-silver IGUs go from $38.50 to $43.90/sq ft, effective May 4, 2026.
- **Seineix's argument.** Seineix has a strong argument that the increase took effect on May 4, 2026. It can also argue that the benchmarking and termination remedy is gone.
- **Exposure on withheld amounts.** Leilisk is paying Column A and treating the difference as disputed (OF §3.4). The withheld differential is building up. If Seineix prevails, all of it becomes payable, and late-payment interest may be claimed (SA §5.6).
- **Limited protection from the reservation.** The reservation of rights preserves Leilisk's arguments. It does not cure the late objection.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Do **not** describe the April 20 objection as timely in any correspondence.
2. Test the notice for defects that could restart or defeat the 30-day clock under SA §5.2:
   - whether it stated the affected products, prices, effective date and a "reasonable explanation of the cost drivers";
   - whether it was delivered to the OF notice address in a manner permitted by SA §19.1 (by hand, courier, or email with confirmation of transmission);
   - whether this was the only adjustment in Contract Year 3; and
   - whether the effective date was at least 60 days after receipt.
3. Rely on the OF §3.3 reservation and on Seineix having entered the restated OF and continued billing at both prices. Use these to negotiate either a signed written waiver of the deadline, so that benchmarking can proceed, or a pricing amendment.
4. Consider folding this into the change-of-control consent negotiation (Issue 1).
5. Calendar a firm internal 30-day deadline from receipt of any future Price Adjustment Notice.

---

### Issue 3: The Quality Agreement's narrow "Defect" definition cuts down the 10-year IGU warranty

**Where:**
- QA §1.4 ("Defect")
- SA §21.2 (Order of Precedence)
- SA §1.1 ("Defect") and §9.1 (IGU Warranty)

**What the documents say:**
- **The warranty.** SA §9.1 warrants IGUs free from Defects for **10 years from Delivery**.
- **The SA definition.** SA §1.1 defines "Defect" broadly. It expressly includes:
  - IGU edge-seal failure (fogging, moisture intrusion, gas loss);
  - coating degradation; and
  - **nickel-sulfide spontaneous breakage**.
- **The QA definition.** QA §1.4 defines "Defect" as a deviation from the Specifications **"detectable by visual inspection"** under ASTM C1036/C1048 **"at the time of Delivery."**
- **Which prevails.** SA §21.2 provides that the QA **"shall prevail"** as to **"the definition of Defect."**

**Why it matters:**
- **Warranty reduced to delivery-day defects.** Read together, the documents limit the 10-year warranty to defects visible on delivery. Those defects will in practice be caught at receiving inspection within 10 Business Days (QA §6.1).
- **Latent failures excluded.** The latent failures the warranty was meant to cover fall outside it: seal failure, coating degradation and NiS breakage. These are the main long-tail risks for a curtain-wall fabricator and its owner warranties. This contradicts TS §8.2, which expressly listed them.
- **Other provisions affected.** The same narrowing affects:
  - the 5-year warranty on other products (SA §9.2); and
  - Seineix's indemnity for injury and property damage "caused by a Defect" (SA §12.1(a)), which matters for falling glass from NiS breakage.
- **Weak fallback only.** Leilisk can argue that latent failures breach the general conformity warranty in SA §9.3(a), because the Specifications incorporate ASTM E2190. That argument is uncertain and should not be relied on.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend SA §21.2 (and conform QA §1.4) so that the QA definition applies **only to receiving inspection and rejection**.
2. Provide that the SA §1.1 definition governs warranty (SA §9) and indemnity (SA §12) claims.
3. Alternatively, rename the QA term (for example, "Visual Nonconformance").
4. Pending the amendment, preserve all warranty claim notices and document latent failures promptly.

---

### Issue 4: Exclusivity is far broader than the Term Sheet deal

**Where:**
- SA §3.1 (Exclusive Purchasing) and §1.1 ("Glass Products", "Affiliate")
- Compare TS §4.1–4.2

**What the documents say:**
- **The SA.** Leilisk and its Affiliates must buy **100%** of their requirements of **all Glass Products** "exclusively from Supplier" for every project **"anywhere in North America."** They may not even solicit quotations from others. "Glass Products" covers monolithic, laminated, fire-rated glass and IGUs, coated or uncoated.
- **The Term Sheet.** The TS limited exclusivity to **triple-silver low-E IGUs for projects in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut**. It left all other products and territories free.

**Why it matters:**
- **No sourcing freedom.** Leilisk cannot source any glass type anywhere in North America elsewhere, or even benchmark prices by obtaining quotes. That undercuts its pricing leverage, which is particularly significant given the 2026 increase (Issue 2).
- **Affects existing operations.** The Allentown, Pennsylvania facility (OF §7.4) is already outside the TS territory.
- **Narrow escape routes.** The only exits are:
  - Seineix's written inability to supply (§3.2);
  - force majeure lasting more than 60 days (§18.1); and
  - owner-specified products, which require notice only (§3.3).
- **Ostrander group.** As noted in Issue 1, the clause extends to the Ostrander group after closing.
- **The Term Sheet does not help.** The TS was expressly non-binding (TS §12.1), and SA §21.3 supersedes prior term sheets. **The TS narrower scope does not bind Seineix or limit SA §3.1.** It is useful only as negotiating evidence of the agreed deal.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Seek a written amendment to SA §3.1 limiting exclusivity to triple-silver low-E IGUs for NY/NJ/CT projects, consistent with TS §4.
2. Add an express right to obtain competitive quotations.
3. Carve out Affiliates, or at least post-closing Ostrander entities.
4. Pending the amendment, Leilisk should not buy other glass from third parties, since that would be a breach.

---

### Issue 5: Automatic 60-month renewal with a 10-Business-Day opt-out window

**Where:**
- SA §2.2 (Renewal) and §1.1 ("Renewal Term", "Opt-Out Period")
- OF §2.2–2.3 (Term)

**What the documents say:**
- **Automatic renewal.** The SA "will renew automatically for successive Renewal Terms." It can be stopped only by notice given during the Opt-Out Period. Both terms are defined by reference to the Order Form.
- **The OF terms.**
  - Renewal Term: **60 months**.
  - Opt-Out Period: **the ten (10) Business Days immediately preceding the 180th day before the end of the then-current term**.
- **What carries over.** SA §3 (exclusivity) and §4 (the 400,000 sq ft minimum and shortfall) continue in each Renewal Term.

**Why it matters:**
- **Lock-in.** Missing a two-week window roughly six months before expiry locks Leilisk into another five years of full exclusivity and minimum-volume commitments.
- **No other exit.** Leilisk has no convenience termination right.
- **The current window.** The Initial Term ends in January 2029. On my count the window falls on approximately **July 5–18, 2028**, allowing for the July 4 bank holiday. The exact dates should be confirmed against the precise expiry date (January 14 or 15, 2029).
- **Notice formalities.** Notice outside the window is ineffective. It must also comply with SA §19.1, and email notice is received on the next Business Day.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Docket the July 2028 window now, with reminders several months in advance.
2. Consider serving non-renewal at the opening of the window.
3. In the amendment package, negotiate:
   - renewal terms of 12 months;
   - an opt-out right exercisable at any time up to 90–180 days before expiry; and
   - preferably, a right to terminate for convenience on notice during any Renewal Term.

---

## 3. Other documents

- **Seineix press release (Sept. 9, 2025).** This is background on the Coater 2 capacity expansion. It raises no issue for Leilisk. It may marginally weaken any capacity-based argument under SA §3.2 and is mildly useful context on cost drivers in the price negotiation.
- **Mutual NDA (Aug. 21, 2023).** This is a pre-deal confidentiality agreement. Its disclosure period ended in August 2025, and its obligations run to August 2028. Ongoing confidentiality is governed by SA §15. No action is needed beyond noting that the Ostrander diligence disclosures should respect SA §15 and the NDA.

## 4. Recommended next steps (in priority order)

1. **This week:** confirm the consent status with deal counsel, and request Seineix's written change-of-control consent and waiver before closing (Issue 1).
2. Review the March 2026 Price Adjustment Notice and its delivery record for defects, then open negotiations on a deadline waiver or pricing amendment (Issue 2).
3. Package a single amendment covering:
   - the warranty "Defect" precedence fix (Issue 3);
   - narrowed exclusivity, including an Affiliate/Ostrander carve-out (Issue 4); and
   - shorter renewal terms and a wider opt-out window (Issue 5).

   The consent request (Issue 1) gives Leilisk a natural occasion to raise this package, although the consent itself should not be held up for it.
4. Docket the July 2028 opt-out window.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Leilisk Facade Systems, Inc. / Seineix Glassworks LLC: Issues in the Supply Arrangement

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed all six documents in the folder:

- Supply Agreement dated January 15, 2024 (New York law)
- October 18, 2023 Term Sheet
- Quality Agreement dated January 15, 2024
- Amended and Restated Order Form No. 1 dated May 11, 2026
- Seineix press release of September 9, 2025
- August 2023 Mutual NDA

**Key commercial terms:**

- **Initial Term:** 60 months (five years) from the January 15, 2024 Effective Date, so it runs to January 2029 (Supply Agreement §2.1; Order Form §2.1).
- **Minimum purchase commitment:** Leilisk must buy at least 400,000 square feet of Glass Products per Contract Year (Supply Agreement §4.1; Order Form §5.1).
- **Shortfall payment:** $4.25 per square foot for any shortfall (Supply Agreement §4.3; Order Form §5.2).

**Four issues need attention.** In order of urgency:

1. The price-adjustment objection was late.
2. The 10-year IGU warranty has been cut down by the Quality Agreement's definition of "Defect."
3. The exclusivity clause is much broader than the deal in the term sheet.
4. The agreement renews automatically for five years at a time, and the window to opt out is narrow.

The press release and the NDA raise no live issues. The press release is marketing material. The NDA's disclosure period ended in August 2025, and for this relationship it has been superseded by Supply Agreement §15.

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1: Price adjustment objection was untimely (deemed acceptance risk)

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement §5.3 (Objection)
- Order Form §3.2–3.4 (Pricing Basis)

**What it says:**
- Leilisk received Seineix's Price Adjustment Notice on **March 4, 2026**. The notice covers all IGUs and laminated glass, with price increases of roughly 10–14%, effective May 4, 2026.
- Under §5.3, Leilisk could object "within thirty (30) days after its receipt." If it did not, the adjustment is "deemed accepted."
- The 30-day window closed on **April 3, 2026**.
- Leilisk's objection letter is dated **April 20, 2026**, which is 17 days late.

**Why it matters:**
- Seineix can argue the higher Column B prices took effect on May 4, 2026.
- Seineix can also argue that Leilisk has lost its §5.3 remedies:
  - benchmarking against three other North American suppliers; and
  - the right to terminate the affected products, which would remove them from exclusivity (§3.1) and the minimum commitment (§4.1).
- Leilisk is currently paying Column A prices under Order Form §3.4. That means a disputed balance is building on every IGU and laminated-glass invoice. If Seineix wins the point, Leilisk will owe that balance, possibly with 1% monthly interest under §5.6 if the amounts are found not to have been disputed in good faith.
- §21.4 provides that a failure or delay in enforcing a right is not a waiver. This weakens any argument that Seineix waived the deadline by later conduct.

**Mitigating points:**
- Leilisk has not accepted the increase. It signed the Order Form "under reservation of rights" and expressly did not accept Column B pricing (§3.3).
- Seineix agreed to dual-column invoicing, with Leilisk paying Column A, pending agreement (§3.4).

**Recommended fix:**
1. Do not concede the point in correspondence.
2. Check the notice against Supply Agreement §5.2:
   - Was it the only adjustment in the Contract Year?
   - Did it state the affected products, the adjusted prices, the effective date, and a "reasonable explanation" of the cost drivers?
   - Was it delivered to the notice address and by a method permitted under §19.1? Confirm the receipt date, because that date starts the 30-day clock.
   - Any defect in the notice may mean the 30-day period never started.
3. Use the §3.4 standstill and Seineix's agreement to dual invoicing to negotiate either:
   - a signed written waiver of the §5.3 deadline that reinstates benchmarking; or
   - a negotiated pricing amendment.
4. Reserve the disputed amounts and calendar all future objection windows strictly.

### Issue 2: Quality Agreement "Defect" definition cuts down the 10-year IGU warranty

**Where:**
- Quality Agreement §1.4 (definition of "Defect")
- Supply Agreement §21.2 (Order of Precedence), §1.1 ("Defect") and §9.1 (IGU Warranty)

**What it says:**
- Supply Agreement §9.1 warrants IGUs free from Defects for **10 years from Delivery**.
- Supply Agreement §1.1 defines "Defect" broadly to include:
  - IGU edge-seal failure;
  - coating degradation; and
  - nickel-sulfide spontaneous breakage.
- Quality Agreement §1.4 defines "Defect" as a deviation from the Specifications "detectable by visual inspection" under ASTM C1036/C1048 "at the time of Delivery."
- Supply Agreement §21.2 provides that the Quality Agreement "shall prevail as to … the definition of Defect."

**Why it matters:**
- Read together, the narrow Quality Agreement definition controls. The 10-year warranty would then cover only defects visible on the day of Delivery.
- Those defects are already handled by the 10-business-day receiving inspection.
- The latent risks a facade fabricator actually faces would fall outside the warranty:
  - seal failure and fogging;
  - coating degradation; and
  - nickel-sulfide breakage years after installation.
- The same narrowing likely affects:
  - the 5-year warranty on other glass (§9.2);
  - the reglazing and access cost reimbursement (§9.4); and
  - the Supplier indemnity for injury or property damage "caused by a Defect" (§12.1(a)).
- The term sheet (§8.2) expressly contemplated coverage of these latent failures. However, the entire-agreement clause (§21.3) means the term sheet cannot be relied on.
- Leilisk's warranties to project owners almost certainly run longer than visual-at-delivery. That leaves an unhedged pass-through gap.

**Recommended fix:**
Negotiate a written amendment under Supply Agreement §21.4 and Quality Agreement §11.3. Either:
- revise §21.2 so the Quality Agreement controls the definition of "Defect" only for inspection and acceptance at Delivery, and the Supply Agreement §1.1 definition governs Sections 9 and 12; or
- rename the Quality Agreement term (for example, "Visual Nonconformance").

Until the amendment is signed, review any pending or anticipated latent-defect claims and preserve Leilisk's position that §8.1 ("Acceptance … does not waive Buyer's rights under Section 9") shows the parties intended the warranty to extend beyond visual defects.

### Issue 3: Exclusivity far broader than the agreed deal

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement §3.1 (Exclusive Purchasing), read with §1.1 ("Glass Products")
- Compare Term Sheet §4

**What it says:**
- §3.1 requires Leilisk and its Affiliates to buy **100% of their requirements of all Glass Products** "exclusively from Supplier" for every project "**anywhere in North America**."
- Leilisk and its Affiliates may not even solicit quotes from or qualify other suppliers.
- "Glass Products" covers all architectural glass: monolithic, laminated, fire-rated and IGUs, whether coated or uncoated.
- The term sheet limited exclusivity to **triple-silver low-E IGUs for projects in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut**. It expressly left Leilisk free to source everything else, and all glass for other projects, from any supplier (Term Sheet §4.2).

**Why it matters:**
- Leilisk cannot competitively source any glass type, or any project outside the tri-state area. This includes work supplied from its Allentown, Pennsylvania facility.
- It loses pricing leverage, which is particularly significant given the disputed 2026 increase.
- The term sheet gives no protection:
  - it was expressly non-binding (Term Sheet preamble and §12.1); and
  - Supply Agreement §21.3 supersedes all prior term sheets.
- The only exits from exclusivity are narrow:
  - Supplier capacity failure (§3.2), order by order;
  - force majeure lasting more than 60 days (§18.1); and
  - owner-specified products, but §3.3 requires only notice and does not clearly permit the purchase.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Seek an amendment narrowing §3.1 to the term-sheet scope: triple-silver low-E IGUs for NY/NJ/CT projects.
2. Add an express carve-out allowing Leilisk to buy owner-specified products.
3. Delete the restriction on soliciting quotes.
4. If Seineix resists, consider fallbacks:
   - a regional limit;
   - a product-category limit; or
   - a price-competitiveness release, allowing Leilisk to buy elsewhere where a third party beats Seineix's price by a set percentage.
5. Audit current sourcing for any existing non-Seineix purchases that may already breach §3.1.

### Issue 4: Five-year evergreen renewal with a 10-business-day opt-out window

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement §2.2 (Renewal)
- Order Form §2.2–2.3 (Term)

**What it says:**
- On expiry of the Initial Term, the agreement will "renew automatically for successive Renewal Terms" unless a party gives non-renewal notice "during the Opt-Out Period."
- The Order Form sets each **Renewal Term at 60 months**.
- The Order Form sets the **Opt-Out Period as the ten (10) Business Days immediately preceding the 180th day before the end of the then-current term**.
- §2.2 confirms that Sections 3 (exclusivity) and 4 (minimum purchase) continue to apply in every Renewal Term.

**Why it matters:**
- If Leilisk misses a ten-business-day window, it is locked in for another five years. That five years would carry:
  - the 400,000 sq ft annual minimum with $4.25/sq ft shortfall exposure; and
  - the overbroad North America exclusivity.
- Notice given early (before the window) or late (after it) is ineffective.
- On my calculation, for the Initial Term ending January 2029:
  - the 180th day before expiry is about July 19, 2028; and
  - the window is approximately **July 5–18, 2028**, allowing for the July 4 holiday.
- The exact dates should be confirmed, because it is not settled whether the term ends on January 14 or January 15, 2029.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Docket the July 2028 window now, with multiple reminders and backup responsibility.
2. Negotiate an amendment to the Order Form (and §2.2 as needed) providing for:
   - renewal terms of 12 months;
   - an opt-out period that runs from, say, 12 months to 90 days before expiry, with notice at any time in that period effective; and
   - ideally, renewal only by mutual written agreement.
3. Package this amendment with the exclusivity amendment, because the renewal multiplies the exclusivity problem.

---

## 3. Suggested Next Steps

1. **Immediately:**
   - Audit the March 4, 2026 Price Adjustment Notice for defects.
   - Confirm the receipt date.
   - Open discussions with Seineix on a written waiver or pricing amendment.
2. **Near term:**
   - Propose a single amendment package covering exclusivity scope, the Defect definition and precedence clause, and the renewal mechanics.
3. **Docketing:**
   - Calendar the July 2028 opt-out window.
   - Calendar future 30-day price-objection deadlines.

Please let me know if you would like a draft amendment or a client-facing summary.
